strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant efficiency issue in Neural CDEs and proposes an intuitive combination of smoothed control paths, multiple views, and attention. Using GP posterior means as CDE controls and attention-dependent observation noise is a potentially useful architectural idea.

The empirical results report sizeable gains on three datasets: MVC-CDE (GP) obtains the highest listed accuracy while reducing wall-clock time and NFE substantially relative to the linear and cubic CDE implementations. Five-seed reporting, tolerance sweeps, noise perturbations, bandwidth/head-count studies, and computational breakdowns are useful evaluation components.
The manuscript is generally organized and readable, with equations, diagrams, a consolidated results table, and substantial implementation detail in the appendix.
The work uses public classification benchmarks and presents no apparent material ethical risk. Its attempt to improve computational efficiency could reduce resource use.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central theory is not valid as stated. Theorem 3.1 claims that NFE is strictly determined by a quasi-norm of the control path's (p+1)-st derivative. Higher derivatives of the CDE solution also depend nonlinearly on the learned vector field and all its relevant derivatives, the evolving state, error norm and scale, rejected steps, and solver implementation; Lipschitz continuity and boundedness do not justify the asserted proportionality. The subsequent NFE conclusions therefore do not follow.

The spline analysis is inconsistent with the theorem it invokes. An order-5 Dormand-Prince argument involving sixth derivatives cannot directly yield the stated total-variation formula for piecewise-linear paths or the second-difference formula for cubic splines, whose relevant derivatives have knot discontinuities. Rough forcing can cause small error-controlled steps, but calling this numerical stiffness and claiming the path geometry alone determines NFE are substantial overstatements.

The smoothing bounds are also insufficiently justified. A Nadaraya-Watson derivative bound requires control of the normalizing denominator and sampling design, while a GP posterior-mean bound must account for coefficients involving (K+Sigma)^{-1}, noise, conditioning, and observation locations. Consequently, the claimed universal NFE proportionality to h^{-1} and independence from noise and sampling density are unsupported. Likewise, the minimum-bandwidth theorem ignores vector-field dynamics, head dimension, and the solver's scaled aggregate error norm.

The GP optimality argument applies only under a correctly specified GP prior and noise model, so it does not establish universally superior reconstruction of an unknown real signal. The claim of strictly lower error everywhere is too strong, and reconstruction fidelity itself is not shown to imply better task performance.

There is a major implementation/reproducibility ambiguity: attention scores are produced by trainable queries and, for MVC-CDE, a trainable CNN; these scores define Sigma and hence the GP inverse. The paper nevertheless describes GP fitting as static, one-time preprocessing with negligible overhead. If attention changes during training, the inverses and paths must be recomputed differentiably; if paths are precomputed, the attention mechanism cannot be trained as described. The manuscript does not resolve this inconsistency or explain how the reported timings were obtained.

The evaluation does not adequately support the broad significance and state-of-the-art claims. All three experiments use regular time grids despite irregular sampling being the main motivation; only three classification datasets are evaluated; standard archive splits appear to be replaced by random 60/20/20 splits; and comparisons omit strong modern discrete and continuous-time models. Several baseline results are surprisingly weak, and the paper supplies neither code nor enough low-level implementation detail to audit them.

Accuracy gains are confounded by model capacity and the added CNN. Each head has its own vector field, but parameter counts and matched-capacity controls are absent. There is no CNN-only or comparably parameterized spline-CDE baseline, so the large MVC-versus-MV improvement cannot be attributed specifically to attentive recovery from smoothing. NFE is also not directly comparable when one evaluation processes several head-specific vector fields.

Experimental reporting contains inconsistencies and omissions: Appendix B.6 says the same UWave tolerance is used uniformly, whereas Table 1 gives cubic CDE a different tolerance; the bandwidth search protocol and selection budget are vague; uncertainty is not identified as standard deviation or standard error; statistical tests are absent; and the noise study is largely graphical without numerical summaries.

Presentation is polished at a high level, but repeated claims such as “strictly determined,” “decouples integration cost from input noise,” and “SOTA” exceed the evidence. The paper also lacks a meaningful limitations discussion covering cubic GP scaling, memory, dynamic path construction, regular-grid-only evidence, and potential loss of predictive high-frequency information. The generic impact statement is adequate for these low-risk benchmarks but does not substitute for such limitations. Overall, the idea has merit, but the unsupported theoretical foundation and unresolved implementation/evaluation issues prevent reliable acceptance.

The evaluation reports accuracy, wall-clock time, and NFE over five seeds. It includes single-path kernel and GP variants, multi-view variants, noise perturbations, head-count studies, bandwidth comparisons, and runtime breakdowns.
The reported empirical results are promising: MVC-GP reaches 95.07%, 98.28%, and 95.39% accuracy on the three datasets while substantially reducing NFE relative to linear and cubic CDEs.
The high-level motivation, architecture, diagrams, and main result table are generally understandable, and the appendix attempts to expose preprocessing and optimization settings.
weaknesses: The central theoretical argument is unsound. Theorem 3.1 claims that NFE is strictly determined by a quasi-norm of the control path's (p+1)-st derivative. Higher derivatives of the CDE solution also contain derivatives and products involving the learned vector field and lower derivatives of the path. Actual adaptive-solver behavior further depends on error norms, state scale, rejected steps, knot handling, and tolerances. The asserted proportionality does not follow from the local truncation-error formula.

The spline consequences contradict the stated theorem. For a fifth-order solver, the analysis invokes a sixth derivative, yet the paper later assigns linear-spline cost to first differences and cubic-spline cost to second differences without deriving this change. Linear paths are nonsmooth at knots and cubic splines are only C2, so the smooth LTE argument cannot be applied as written. Equations (9) and (11) are unsupported.

Theorem 3.2 is also not established. A Nadaraya-Watson estimator is a normalized quotient whose derivative bound depends on its denominator and sampling geometry. A GP posterior mean has coefficients involving (K+Sigma)^{-1}, so its derivatives depend on noise and matrix conditioning, not only h and the magnitude of the observations. Consequently, the claimed h^{-1} NFE law and independence from input noise do not follow. The 'strictly optimal' GP comparison additionally holds only under the assumed, correctly specified GP prior, not for an arbitrary true signal.

The claimed multi-head bottleneck theorem ignores trajectory amplitudes, vector fields, solver error normalization, and the increasing per-evaluation cost with the number of heads. NFE alone therefore cannot establish total computational complexity, and it is not strictly governed by the smallest bandwidth.

There is a serious implementation/runtime ambiguity. In the proposed GP model, learned attention determines a per-example, per-head covariance Sigma_m, so the inverse in Equation (4) changes during training and seemingly requires differentiable O(MN^3) computation on each forward pass. The paper nevertheless describes GP fitting as static one-time preprocessing and reports only negligible fitting overhead. It does not explain an approximation, caching strategy, or implementation that reconciles these statements.

The empirical scope is too narrow for the broad claims: only three classification datasets are used, all are converted to regular unit-spaced grids, and no missing-data or genuinely irregular-sampling experiment is presented despite this being the main Neural CDE motivation. The 'state-of-the-art' claim is unsupported by comparisons to the broader time-series classification literature; even among reported baselines, GRU-D is much faster and competitive on two datasets.

The accuracy comparison is confounded. MVC-GP adds a two-layer 128-channel CNN, multiple trajectories, and apparently separate vector fields, but parameter counts, FLOPs, and CNN-only or capacity-matched controls are absent. Global softmax attention processes the complete sequence before constructing every point of the path, so it can encode label-relevant information and is not causal in the sense claimed by the paper. The large gain from MV-GP to MVC-GP could therefore arise from the added discrete encoder rather than improved CDE path reconstruction.

Hyperparameter fairness and reporting are insufficient. Proposed bandwidths are swept over a broad range, while spline CDEs are forced to share the proposed models' learning schedule; tuning budgets are not matched. The text claims heterogeneous bandwidths are superior, but the selected main models use identical bandwidths on two datasets. The UWave cubic tolerance in Table 1 also conflicts with the supposedly uniform setting in Appendix B.6.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code or execution artifact is provided, and important details are missing, including exact random splits and seeds, the complete bandwidth search, whether bandwidths are learned, vector-field sharing, initialization and readout for multiple heads, GP derivative evaluation, numerical linear-algebra stabilization, parameter counts, and precise timing protocol.

The presentation repeatedly overstates evidence using terms such as 'strictly determined,' 'fundamental,' and 'SOTA.' There is no substantive limitations section discussing cubic GP scaling, non-causality, suppression of task-relevant high-frequency events, or restriction to short offline classification. The generic impact statement is weak, although the public benchmark experiments do not raise an unresolved material ethical concern. Overall, the method is promising, but unsupported core theory and insufficiently controlled evidence prevent acceptance.

strengths: The core idea—reducing Neural CDE solver cost by smoothing the driving path—is intuitive, practically relevant, and offers a useful alternative to modifying the solver or latent dynamics.
The multi-view construction is reasonably original: learned queries create several weighted smooth paths, and the convolutional extension uses local context to determine observation importance.
The empirical results are promising. Across three datasets, Table 1 reports large reductions in NFE and wall-clock time alongside improved accuracy, with five-seed means and standard deviations.
The paper includes useful head-count, bandwidth, noise-robustness, tolerance, and computational-breakdown studies. Its figures are legible and the overall method is presented clearly.
No major ethical concern is apparent for the benchmark-classification experiments.
weaknesses: The central theoretical analysis is not sound as stated. Theorem 3.1 claims that NFE is strictly determined by a quasi-norm of the control path's (p+1)-st derivative. Higher derivatives of the CDE solution also depend on the vector field and its derivatives, lower-order derivatives of the control, state magnitude, solver norm, and tolerances; they are not generally proportional to X^(p+1). Consequently, the subsequent linear-spline, cubic-spline, and h^(-1) NFE laws are not established.

Theorem 3.2's bound is inadequately justified and appears false without substantial additional assumptions. Differentiating a normalized Nadaraya-Watson estimator introduces derivatives of its denominator, while a GP posterior derivative also depends on the inverse Gram matrix, observation noise, and sampling geometry. These factors cannot generally be absorbed into a kernel-only constant independent of the observation locations.

The paper repeatedly calls rough or rapidly varying forcing 'stiffness,' but these are not equivalent numerical phenomena. Theorem 3.4 also discusses NFE only, ignoring that each evaluation of the concatenated M-head system is substantially more expensive and apparently uses M separate 128-dimensional vector fields.

The computational account is internally unclear. Attention-dependent GP noise matrices change as the learned queries and CNN change, so GP trajectory fitting cannot simply be a static, one-time preprocessing operation unless gradients or paths are treated in an undocumented way. The reported sub-second trajectory-fitting overhead for multiple per-sample GP inversions therefore needs an exact algorithm and complexity explanation.

The accuracy comparison is confounded by capacity and architecture. MVC-CDE adds a two-layer 128-channel CNN and multiple independent 128-dimensional CDE states/vector fields, but parameter counts, FLOPs, and matched-capacity baselines are absent. A CNN-only classifier and controls using the CNN representation without attentive GP paths are necessary to attribute the gains to the proposed mechanism.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the motivation: only three classification datasets are tested, all represented on regular integer grids. There are no missing-data or genuinely irregular-sampling experiments, despite these being central motivations for Neural CDEs.

The claimed state-of-the-art accuracy is not supported by comparisons against contemporary strong time-series classifiers. The evaluation includes mainly differential-equation baselines, and the authors create random 60/20/20 splits rather than using established archive splits, limiting comparability and potentially introducing dataset-specific leakage. Statistical significance tests are also absent.

Several fairness and reporting issues remain: UWave's cubic tolerance is 1e-3 in Table 1 despite Section B.6 stating 1e-4 uniformly for cubic and proposed models; fixed, dataset-dependent epoch budgets do not establish equal convergence; and the headline inference-speed claim is not supported by a dedicated latency or throughput table.

Reproducibility is insufficient for ICML acceptance: no code or pseudocode is provided, important implementation details for differentiable GP construction and solver batching are missing, parameter counts and exact search/selection procedures are unreported, and the bandwidth notation is inconsistent between raw factors, effective scales, and 'LS' values.

The manuscript lacks a substantive limitations discussion. The boilerplate impact statement does not address cubic GP scaling, dependence on bandwidth selection, regular-grid-only evidence, additional multi-head capacity, or potential failure when high-frequency signal components are genuinely predictive.

strengths: Originality/significance: Targeting control-path regularity as an efficiency lever for Neural CDEs is a useful direction. Combining multiple smoothed paths with query-based weighting and a convolutional attention front end is a reasonably original architectural contribution with potential practical value.

Empirical breadth: The paper reports five-seed results, accuracy, wall-clock time, NFE, memory, noise robustness, missing-observation experiments, solver-order comparisons, head-count ablations, and a smoothing-spline baseline. On the reported experiments, MVC-GP often substantially reduces NFE and improves accuracy over the authors' spline CDE implementations.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized, motivates the accuracy-efficiency trade-off clearly, and provides readable diagrams and extensive appendices. The component-wise results help distinguish single-path smoothing, multi-view attention, and convolutional feature extraction.

Limitations and ethics: The discussion honestly identifies bandwidth sensitivity, loss of high-frequency information, adaptive-solver dependence, and the stiffest-head bottleneck. The work appears low-risk and raises no material ethical concern, although its impact statement is generic.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central theoretical analysis is not valid as stated. Theorem 3.1 infers an upper bound on NFE from a local-error step-size constraint in the wrong direction and asserts that NFE is 'strictly determined' by a derivative quasi-norm. In fact, solution derivatives also depend on the vector field and its higher derivatives, lower derivatives of the control, the evolving state, the solver controller, rejected steps, and error-norm scaling. The claim that state derivatives scale linearly with only the corresponding derivative of X is unjustified.

Soundness: The spline analysis is inconsistent with the purported theorem. For a fifth-order Dormand-Prince method, Theorem 3.1 invokes the sixth derivative, whereas the cubic-spline estimate is based on second finite differences; a piecewise cubic has zero higher derivatives inside intervals and derivative discontinuities at knots. Likewise, the stated linear- and cubic-spline NFE formulas do not follow from the preceding argument.

Soundness: Theorem 3.2 treats finite-sample Nadaraya-Watson and GP posterior means as simple convolutions. Derivatives of the Nadaraya-Watson normalization introduce denominator and sampling-grid dependence, while GP posterior derivatives depend on (K+sigma^2 I)^{-1}, its conditioning, noise, and sample locations. Consequently, the claimed uniform bound independent of these quantities and the resulting NFE proportional to h^{-1} corollary are unsupported. The GP 'strictly more accurate' result is only Bayes-optimal under the assumed, correctly specified GP prior, not a general reconstruction guarantee.

Methodological consistency: MVC-GP's attention weights are learned and determine a sample- and head-specific noise matrix Sigma. Thus the GP inverse changes as the attention parameters change and apparently must be recomputed during training. This conflicts with the characterization of GP fitting as a static, one-time preprocessing cost. The implementation needed to reconcile this issue is not described, undermining both the method specification and the reported computational interpretation.

Evaluation: The state-of-the-art claim is not supported. Only three main classification datasets are used, with custom random 60/20/20 splits instead of the archives' standard splits, and the comparison omits many strong modern time-series classifiers. Linear and cubic CDEs are forced to use the proposed methods' optimization schedules, while several other baselines receive separate tuning; the proposed methods additionally receive broad bandwidth, head-count, and architecture searches. This does not establish a fair SOTA comparison.

Evaluation: The forecasting evidence is one dataset, one short context/horizon, one missingness setting, and only basic GRU and cubic-CDE comparators. It is insufficient for the broad forecasting and online-deployment claims. Global smoothing and attention are noncausal; repeatedly refitting them in rolling windows is suggested but end-to-end streaming latency is not evaluated.

Reproducibility: No code or artifact is provided, and important details are missing, including vector-field depth and widths, attention/context dimensions, whether bandwidths are fixed or learned, the exact GP computation and stabilization, solver error norm and adjoint setup, split identities, and the full validation-search protocol. The reported hardware also changes between the L40 setup and the H100 timing breakdown, complicating efficiency comparisons.

Presentation/claims: The paper repeatedly calls rough or nonsmooth forcing 'stiffness,' although stiffness has a more specific numerical meaning and is not established here. It also claims to decouple integration cost from noise despite the invalid theory and finite empirical coverage. These overstatements materially obscure what the experiments actually demonstrate.

Overall, the underlying idea is promising and the reported empirical trends merit further study, but invalid central theorems, an unresolved dynamic-GP cost inconsistency, and an insufficiently controlled evaluation prevent the methodology and efficiency claims from being relied upon. These issues require substantial revision rather than a minor clarification.

strengths: The core empirical motivation is useful: replacing exact interpolation with smoother control paths can substantially reduce adaptive-solver work. Table 2 reports large NFE and wall-clock reductions relative to linear and cubic Neural CDEs, especially on UWaveGestureLibrary.

The proposed multi-view construction is a sensible attempt to recover predictive information lost through smoothing. The single-path, multi-view, convolutional, bandwidth, solver-order, noise, and missing-observation ablations provide several informative comparisons.

Presentation is generally organized and visually clear. The appendix provides dataset descriptions, optimization settings, parameter counts, memory measurements, five-run uncertainty estimates, and an honest limitations section covering bandwidth sensitivity, loss of high-frequency information, solver dependence, and the stiffest-head bottleneck.

The work has moderate originality: combining task-aware smoothing, attention-weighted GP paths, and parallel CDE integration is a potentially useful architectural contribution, even though its ingredients are established.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central theoretical analysis is not valid as stated. In Theorem 3.1, an upper bound on the acceptable step size implies a lower—not upper—bound on the required number of steps. Moreover, higher derivatives of z are not simply proportional to the corresponding derivative of X; they contain derivatives of the vector field and products of lower-order derivatives. Consequently, NFE is not 'strictly determined' by the displayed quasi-norm of X.

The spline analysis is incompatible with the preceding smoothness assumptions. A linear interpolant has derivative discontinuities, and a natural cubic spline is only C2, so the claimed dependence on the (p+1)-st classical derivative for a fifth-order solver cannot directly yield the asserted finite-difference formulas. The paper also repeatedly calls rough forcing 'stiffness' without establishing stiffness in the numerical-analysis sense.

Theorem 3.2 is unsupported for both estimators. Derivatives of a normalized Nadaraya-Watson estimator also depend on its denominator, sample locations, and boundary effects. Derivatives of a GP posterior mean depend on (K+σ²I)^−1X and hence on conditioning, sample count, and noise—not only on h^−p||X||∞. The corollary that NFE is independent of noise and sampling density therefore does not follow.

The GP optimality result applies only when the assumed GP prior and observation model are correct. It does not justify the manuscript's general claim that GP smoothing is maximally faithful to an unknown real signal, nor a universal strict advantage over kernel smoothing.

The efficiency accounting is conceptually incomplete. A block-system NFE counts one solver call even though that call evaluates multiple head-specific vector fields, so equal NFE does not imply equal compute. More importantly, the attentive GP covariance contains learned, input-dependent heteroscedastic noise; its inverse must generally be recomputed during training and cannot be treated as a static one-time preprocessing cost as claimed.

Experimental support is too narrow and inconsistently framed for the broad SOTA and scalability claims. The principal classification evidence covers only three small archive datasets, uses new random 60/20/20 splits rather than established benchmark splits, and omits many strong modern time-series and irregular-sampling baselines. MVC-GP is not even the most accurate method on CharacterTrajectories, where Mamba obtains 96.64% versus 95.07%.

Several evaluation choices weaken comparability. Baselines receive different optimization searches; the spline CDEs are forced to share the proposed method's schedule rather than being independently optimized; the bandwidth search is described only as a broad continuous range; and statistical significance is not tested. Randomly dropping whole timestamps on an otherwise regular grid also does not adequately establish performance for asynchronous, feature-wise irregular observations.

Some reported resource claims are internally questionable: the paper says all models were trained on a single NVIDIA L40, yet Table 3 reports 62,323.94 MB peak VRAM for Mamba, exceeding the standard 48 GB capacity of that GPU. Appendix timing results later switch to an H100, making the end-to-end speed evidence difficult to reconcile.

The claim of suitability for strictly online streaming is not demonstrated. Global kernel/GP smoothing requires the complete history window, and repeatedly refitting it in rolling windows is only proposed rather than benchmarked for incremental latency. The forecasting experiment contains only one dataset, one horizon, one missingness pattern, and three baselines.

Reproducibility is inadequate for acceptance: no code or artifact link is supplied, exact random seeds and split indices are absent, architecture dimensions are incompletely specified, and several implementation details needed to reproduce dynamic GP fitting, batching, interpolation evaluation, timing, and memory measurement are missing.

There are no evident material ethical risks, and the limitations discussion is a positive feature. However, the impact statement is boilerplate and does not discuss failure modes in potentially sensitive irregular time-series applications such as healthcare, despite motivating the work with medical records.

strengths: The core idea—reducing adaptive-solver cost by smoothing the Neural CDE control path, then recovering task-relevant information with multiple attention-weighted paths—is intuitive, practically motivated, and reasonably original.

The empirical section is broader than the three headline classification experiments: it includes noise perturbations, missing observations, head-count and bandwidth studies, solver-order comparisons, a smoothing-spline baseline, memory measurements, and high-dimensional PEMS-SF results.

Reported results are promising. MVC-GP substantially reduces NFE and training time relative to spline CDEs while improving accuracy on the selected datasets; results are averaged over five seeds and parameter counts are approximately matched.
The paper is generally well organized, with readable figures, explicit equations, dataset descriptions, and a useful component-wise discussion of the architecture.

The limitations section honestly identifies bandwidth sensitivity, loss of high-frequency information, the stiffest-head bottleneck, and dependence on adaptive solvers. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central theoretical analysis is not sound as stated. Theorem 3.1 treats high-order derivatives of the CDE solution as proportional to the corresponding derivative of the control path, omitting nonlinear combinations involving derivatives of the vector field and lower-order path derivatives. Moreover, the step-size inequality used in the proof implies a lower bound on the number of steps unless one additionally proves that the controller selects comparable step sizes; the manuscript instead presents an upper bound and claims NFE is 'strictly determined' by the path derivative.

The theory is inconsistent with the interpolants being analyzed. For a fifth-order Dormand–Prince method, a cubic polynomial has vanishing sixth derivative within each interval, so the proposed bound cannot directly produce the later finite-difference estimate for cubic splines. Knot handling, error estimation, rejected steps, learned vector-field stiffness, and solver stability are not incorporated. Calling rough forcing 'stiffness' is also not justified in the numerical-analysis sense.

Theorem 3.2 is inadequately supported and appears false at the stated generality. A normalized Nadaraya–Watson estimator is a ratio rather than a simple convolution, so derivative bounds depend on the denominator, sampling geometry, boundaries, and attention weights. GP posterior derivatives additionally depend on the conditioning of the Gram matrix and coefficients such as (K+Sigma)^{-1}X, not only on h and the observation sup norm. Consequently, the claimed noise-independent NFE scaling does not follow.

The headline 'state-of-the-art' claim is not established. The main comparison covers only three classification datasets and a narrow baseline set, omitting strong modern time-series classifiers and published benchmark results. Several baselines perform unusually poorly or variably—for example ODE-RNN and Log-NCDE on UWave—and proposed models receive extensive bandwidth/head tuning without an equally transparent tuning-budget comparison.

The efficiency evidence does not fully support the abstract's inference-time claim. The main table reports total training-related wall time, while the only inference decomposition is graphical and is collected on different hardware and batch settings. NFE counts a joint multi-head vector-field call as one evaluation even though its cost grows with the number of heads, so NFE alone is not a comparable compute measure.

The treatment of GP cost is unclear. Attention weights are learned and paths are described as dynamically constructed, which seemingly requires repeated sample- and head-specific linear solves rather than a one-time preprocessing operation. The implementation used to obtain the surprisingly small fitting overhead is not specified, and no sequence-length scaling experiment supports the claim that cubic GP construction is negligible.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or repository is identified, seed values and final architecture dimensions are absent, model-selection and bandwidth-search budgets are insufficiently specified, and some tables use different configurations for apparently corresponding results. The use of new random 60/20/20 splits rather than official archive splits also impedes comparison with prior work.

The forecasting evidence is too limited for its claims: it uses one dataset, one horizon and missingness pattern, and only GRU and cubic-CDE baselines. Calling the setup generative or validating low-latency streaming is not warranted by a window-level encoder with global smoothing and no measured rolling-window latency.

Although the acknowledged limitations are useful, the paper does not adequately acknowledge the invalid assumptions in its complexity analysis, the offline/noncausal nature and cubic scaling of GP smoothing, or the limited basis for broad state-of-the-art and scalability claims. These issues affect soundness rather than merely presentation and require substantial revision before acceptance.
